claims.text: Blue pottery of Jaipur is based on ground quartz, and its GI application calls it primarily a ceramic body made of quartz.

quotes.quote: Blue Pottery is based on ground quartz.
Blue pottery of Jaipur and its surrounding villages is unique in that primarily it is a ceramic body made of quartz.

claims.text: Outlook Traveller and an artisan interviewed by Urvashi Dev Rawal say the absence of clay is what distinguishes blue pottery.

quotes.quote: The absence of clay is what distinguishes blue pottery from traditional pottery.
He says the distinctive feature of Blue Pottery is that it is not made with clay.

claims.text: The statement of case says the blue on the product is so dominant it is easily recognised, and cobalt-oxide blue is the key shade of its visual appeal.

quotes.quote: The blue colour on the product is so dominant that it can be easily recognised on the naked eye.
The brilliance of blue created from the cobalt oxide is striking and is the key shade to create the visual appeal of these items.

claims.text: The statement of case says the product perhaps owes its name to the prominent use of blue colour, and Outlook Traveller ties the name to the extensive use of cobalt blue dye.

quotes.quote: Perhaps, the product owes its name from the use of blue colour prominently in the process of making of the product.
The term "blue pottery" refers to the extensive use of cobalt blue dye to give the items a striking tint.

claims.text: Blue pottery of Jaipur is completely hand painted, which its GI documents list among its unique features.

quotes.quote: The pottery is completely hand painted.
Some of the unique features of Blue Pottery of Jaipur are it is completely hand painted

claims.text: The GI application describes blue pottery products as quite light in weight, with a surface that shines but is less glossy.

quotes.quote: The blue pottery products are quite light weight. The surface shines but the shine is less glossy.
The products are quite light weight. The surface of the product shines and with less glossy.

claims.text: Blue glaze pottery is a type of ceramics produced in Jaipur, decorated with hand-painted patterns, often floral or geometric, against a distinct blue background.

quotes.quote: A type of ceramics produced in Jaipur, Rajasthan, blue glaze pottery is decorated with hand-painted patterns, often floral or geometric, set against a distinct blue background.

claims.text: Blue pottery is Turko-Persian in origin but is widely known as one of the distinctive crafts of Jaipur.

quotes.quote: Blue Pottery is Turko-Persian in origin, but today is widely known as one of the distinctive crafts of Jaipur.
The magnificent technique of blue pottery, Turko-Persian in origin, reached East India with Turkish conquests in the 14th century and later flourished under Mughal patronage.
It traces its roots to Turko-Persian culture (beginning in the ninth and tenth centuries)

claims.text: The GI documents say blue pottery is practised in many villages of Jaipur district, and the statement of case names families in Jaipur and nearby villages such as Nevta, Muhana, Mahalan and Kotjewar.

quotes.quote: Blue pottery is practiced in many villages in the Jaipur district.
Many families in Jaipur and nearby villages like Sanganeq nevta, Muhana, Mahalan and Kotjewar are actively involved in producing these art works.

claims.text: The CBSE manual says the blue pottery cluster in Jaipur includes the Neota, Mehla, Mohana and KotJewar area.

quotes.quote: In Jaipur the cluster of Blue Pottery includes Neota, Mehla, Mohana and KotJewar area.

claims.text: Besides Jaipur, the pottery is practised in the villages of Neota and Kotjewar and among the Kumhar, Muslim, Natt, Rajput and Regar communities.

quotes.quote: Although Jaipur has been the prominent center, other areas where this style of pottery is practiced include the villages of Neota and Kotjewar near Jaipur and in the communities of Kumhar, Muslim, Natt, Rajput, and Regar.

claims.text: Kot Jewar village lies about 40 km from Jaipur, and The Federal reports that blue pottery has become the lifeblood of its community.

quotes.quote: In the village of Kot Jewar, 40 km from Jaipur, the ancient art of blue pottery has become the lifeblood of the community.
from Kot Jewar to Jaipur, a distance of about 40 km.

claims.text: The GI registration of Blue Pottery of Jaipur covers the geographical area of Rajasthan, in class 21 for handicraft goods.

quotes.quote: | Class | 21 | | Goods | Handicraft | | Geographical Area | Rajasthan |

claims.text: The blue colour derives from jeypoorite and seypoorite, forms of cobalt oxide originally mined in the principality of Khetri in present-day Rajasthan.

quotes.quote: The distinct blue colour is derived from jeypoorite and seypoorite, forms of cobalt oxides that were originally mined in the principality of Khetri (in present-day Rajasthan).
Blue.-Obtained from cobalt from Khetri (Jaipur State).

claims.text: The Jaipur Museum Handbook of 1895 recorded that the cobalt and copper colouring the pottery were found near Bhagore, on the Raja of Khetri's estate.

quotes.quote: The following description is condensed from the Handbook of the Jaipur Museum, which was published in 1895
the cobalt and copper, with which it is coloured, are also found near Bhagore, on the estate of the Raja of Khetri, a Jaipur noble.

claims.text: The Journal of Indian Art says the green came from an oxide of copper found with the cobalt in the same mines.

quotes.quote: The characteristic blue colour is derived from Syepoorite or Jeypoorite, an oxide of cobalt, and the green from an oxide of copper which is associated with it in the same mines.

claims.text: Purple for the pottery was obtained from a stone called saind found in Bharatpur district of present-day Rajasthan.

quotes.quote: purple - obtained from a stone known as saind found in Bharatpur district in present-day Rajasthan
Purple (Bazjnz).-This colour is obtained from Biana in the Bharatpur State from a stone called Saznd.

claims.text: Yellow was made from lead melted with pewter and then mixed with sandstone from Karauli.

quotes.quote: Yellow.-From lead. The lead is melted and mixed with vamg (pewter) to reduce it.
then mixed with sandstone from Karauli and gives the required yellow colour.
yellow - obtained by mixing lead and pewter, and yellow sandstone

claims.text: A solid turquoise ground is made by painting the surface not covered with designs with a mixture of copper oxide and gum.

quotes.quote: If the surface of the vessel not covered with designs should have a turquoise (fhzrozz) colour, it is painted with a preparation made of oxide of copper and gum.
sometimes the entire surface may be treated with a mixture of copper oxide and gum to produce a solid turquoise colour

claims.text: The statement of case says the design is filled in with other metal oxides, each of which is transformed into a bright colour by firing.

quotes.quote: The design is filled in with other metal oxides, each of which is transformed into a bright colour by firing.

claims.text: On firing, the oxide of cobalt becomes deep blue, chromium turns green, cadmium gives bright yellow and iron oxide becomes red-brown.

quotes.quote: The oxide of cobalt becomes a deep blue, that of chromium changes to green, cadmium produces a bright yellow and iron oxide becomes a red-brown.
iron may be used for red, cadmium for yellow and chromium for green

claims.text: The V&A records that the green leaves on a Jaipur jar of about 1880 are painted in copper oxide against a turquoise copper ground.

quotes.quote: These with the green leaves are painted in green (copper oxide) and set against a turquoise (copper) ground.
Earthenware jar and cover, Jaipur, about 1880

claims.text: The CBSE manual says blue pottery is adorned with blue from cobalt oxide, green from copper oxide, and white.

quotes.quote: Blue pottery is adorned with blue colour derived from cobalt oxide, green derived from copper oxide and white

claims.text: Copper oxide gives a light blue and chrome oxide a green, while the statement of case lists manganese for dark brown.

quotes.quote: Blue-Copper Oxide,Green-Chrome Oxide,Dark brown-Manganese.
cobalt oxide produces deep blue, copper oxide creates light blue, chrome oxide results in green

claims.text: Ceramics Monthly lists the Jaipur colours as copper for turquoise, chromium for green, cobalt for dark blue and black, iron for brown, cadmium for yellow and manganese for purple.

quotes.quote: The colors of Jaipur pottery are as follows: copper to create turquoise; chromium to create green; cobalt to create dark blue and black; iron to create brown; cadmium to create yellow; and manganese to create purple.

claims.text: The statement of case says 80 per cent of the quartz is left after firing, and this maintains the form of the vessel.

quotes.quote: All the melts, but 80 per c€nt of the quartz is left, and this maintains the form of the vessel.

claims.text: The glaze raw materials are heated to a high temperature, and borax reduces their melting point.

quotes.quote: These raw materials are heated at a high temperature; melting point is reduced by borax.

claims.text: The glaze is made by heating powdered glass, borax, zinc oxide, potassium nitrate and boric acid together until the mixture melts.

quotes.quote: A combination of powdered glass, borax, zinc oxide, potassium nitrate, and boric acid are mixed together and heated until the mixture melts.
A special glaze is prepared using different raw material like powdered glass, borax, zinc oxide, potassium nitrate, and boric acid.

claims.text: The melted glaze is cooled and ground into a fine powdered frit, which is mixed with maida and water to make the final glaze.

quotes.quote: After it cools, the resulting glass is again ground into a fine-powdered frit and mixed with maida and water to create the final glaze.
Splinters are collected and then grounded. The grounded frit is mixed with water to form glaze

claims.text: After painting, the statement of case says, the piece is dipped into a homemade glaze of glass, borax and lead oxide made adhesive with boiled flour; it lists sindoor (red lead), suhaga (borax powder) and crushed glass.

quotes.quote: the unfired pieces are hand painted with oxide colours, dipped in clear glaze and fired once in wooden kilns.
The piece is then dipped into a homemade glaze of glass, borax and lead oxide which is made adhesive by the addition of boiled flour.
Glaze -,Sindoor (red lead), Suhaga (Borax powder), Crushed glass.

claims.text: The head potter's notes and Impart make the final glaze by melting borax, sindhur or vermilion and glass, then powdering the cooled solid and mixing it with flour paste.

quotes.quote: This glaze is prepared by melting borax, vermilion and glass at high temperatures. Once the solution has cooled and solidified, it is pulverised into a fine powder and mixed with a flour paste to form a thick glaze solution.
Suhaga (borax) ... ... § seefs Sindhur (vermilion)

It is then melted in a crucible and this melted liquid is Sheiwad to cool and solidify. The solid lump is then broken into fine grains and passed through a mill in order to reduce it to a fine powder.

claims.text: A 2003 CGCRI paper reports that its intervention eliminated lead, a toxic material and proven health hazard, from blue pottery and made the body five times stronger.

quotes.quote: Subramanian, R B V (2003) CGCRI gives new life to Jaipur blue pottery - a success story

The technological intervention has not only eliminated lead, a toxic material and a proven health hazard in blue pottery, but made the body five times stronger, eco-friendly, export-worthy and free from other defects of water leakage and glaze blackening.

claims.text: Blue pottery suffered from lead in its body and glaze compositions and from water leakage due to high porosity, fragility and glaze blackening.

quotes.quote: an ailing traditional blue pottery due to contents of lead in the body and glaze compositions
Apart from the presence of lead in compositions, the blue pottery also suffered from defects like water leakage due to higher porosity, fragileness due to lower strength, glaze blackening etc.

claims.text: CSIR reports that CGCRI transferred its high-strength eco-friendly blue pottery glaze technology to artisans in several clusters around Jaipur.

quotes.quote: This lead high strength eco-friendly blue pottery glaze and the technology was transferred to the artisans in several clusters around Jaipur through series of T&D programs as well as implementation at units' level by CGCRI.

claims.text: CSIR reports a lead-free body with about 150% higher dry strength and a lead-free engobe and glaze with about 405% higher fired strength.

quotes.quote: Developed Lead-free Body possessing Dry Strength ~ 150% higher. Developed Blue Pottery with Lead-free Engobe and Glaze having Fired Strength ~ 405% Higher.

claims.text: The Federal reports that lead was traditionally used in the blue pottery glaze, but that modern techniques have shifted towards lead-free coatings.

quotes.quote: Traditionally, lead was used in the glaze, but modern techniques have shifted towards lead-free coatings

claims.text: The Rough Guide to India, quoted by The Federal, warns that Jaipur blue pottery should not be used for hot food as its glazes are unstable and potentially toxic.

quotes.quote: a word of caution comes from author Dave Abram in 'The Rough Guide to India,'
None of it-despite what some shop owners claim-should be used for hot food, as the glazes are unstable and potentially toxic.

claims.text: The GI application says blue pottery does not crack much and is impervious, so it is found very suitable and hygienic for daily use.

quotes.quote: Since it does not crack much and is impervious, it is found very suitable and hygienic for daily use.

claims.text: In a body-part discomfort survey of 30 male blue pottery workers, every worker reported discomfort in the lower back and knee.

quotes.quote: For this assessment 30 male workers are selected using convenient sampling.
It was found that 100 % of workers experienced the discomfort in the lower back and knee.

claims.text: A significant share of blue pottery workers work in poor postures with a high risk of musculoskeletal disorders, a main reason for absenteeism and leaving the profession.

quotes.quote: A significant population of the workers are working in poor postures which have high risk of Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) and is one of the main reason for absenteeism and leaving the profession of blue pottery manufacturing.

claims.text: A 2016 conference paper reports that, as an unorganised sector, blue pottery manufacturing had no statistical data on the number employed or accident rates.

quotes.quote: Budapest, Hungary - August 22 - 23, 2016

Blue pottery manufacturing is one of the famous art in India, very old profession employing many people. As an unorganized sector, no statistical data are available to date such as the number of people employed, accident rates, and other problems.

claims.text: Blue pottery needs only one firing for both baking and glazing, unlike clay pottery, which needs two firings.

quotes.quote: Requires only one firing for baking and glazing unlike clay pottery where two firings are required.
Jaipur potters do not bisque fire their wares

claims.text: By wetting the edges, even dry pieces can be joined, and wetting the attachment area to leather hard prevents cracking between the parts.

quotes.quote: By wetting the edges, even the dry pieces can be joined.
the attachment area is wet with water until it becomes leather hard to ease the transition from completely dry to wet dough and prevent cracking between the two parts

claims.text: Because the dough lacks plasticity, it cannot be hard-pressed on the wheel to make large products, so many objects are made in plaster moulds.

quotes.quote: Because of the low plasticity of the dough, many of the objects in Jaipur blue pottery are made in plaster molds, using press-molding techniques.
The dough used in blue pottery lacks plasticity due to which they can"t be hard-pressed on wheel to make large products.

claims.text: The V&A records that Jaipur School of Art pieces, made of feldspar and starch, could not be thrown on a wheel and were raised by hand or moulded.

quotes.quote: As the pieces were made of a mixture of feldspar and starch they could not be thrown on a wheel but were either raised by hand or shaped in a mould.
As the pieces were made of a mixture of feldspar and starch they could not be thrown on a wheel but were either raised by hand or in a mould.

claims.text: The Jaipur Museum Handbook gave clay and felspar, obtained in Jaipur State, as the principal ingredients of the pottery.

quotes.quote: The clay and felspar, which are the principal ingredients in its manufacture, are, however, obtained in the State

claims.text: The GI application says the quartz composition of the ceramic is well suited to the hot and dry climate of the area.

quotes.quote: The quartz composition of the ceramic is well suited to the hot and dry climate of the area.

claims.text: The Federal reports that production halts during the monsoon because the traditional technique relies on sun-drying, and the CBSE manual lists dependency on the sun for drying among the industry's problems.

quotes.quote: Production halts during the monsoon, as the traditional technique relies on sun-drying, making work impossible during the rainy season.
Some other problems faced by the blue pottery industry are:
7. Dependency on sun for drying.

claims.text: After being dipped in the glaze, the pieces are set in the sun to dry, according to Ceramics Monthly and the CBSE manual.

quotes.quote: After being dipped in the glaze, all pieces are set in the sun to dry.
The final products are dipped in this solution in a way that it gets an even coating. The product is finally dried in sun.

claims.text: In Kot Jewar, blue pottery pieces dry in the abundant sunlight on the rooftops and courtyards of artists' homes.

quotes.quote: where these blue creations claim space on rooftops and courtyards of artists' homes, absorbing the abundant sunlight as part of their careful drying process.

claims.text: Blue glaze on pottery is an imported technique first developed by Mongol artisans who combined Chinese glazing technology with Persian decorative arts.

quotes.quote: The use of blue glaze on pottery made from Multani mitti, or Fuller's earth, is an imported technique, first developed by enterprising Mongol artisans who combined Chinese glazing technology with Persian decorative arts.
Mongol artisans fused Chinese glazing methods with Persian decorative motifs

claims.text: The blue glaze technique travelled to India in the 14th century, with early Muslim rulers and Turkish conquests.

quotes.quote: This technique traveled south to India with early Muslim potentates in the 14th century.
The magnificent technique of blue pottery, Turko-Persian in origin, reached East India with Turkish conquests in the 14th century

claims.text: In its infancy the blue glaze technique was used to make tiles to decorate mosques, tombs and palaces in Central Asia.

quotes.quote: During its infancy, it was used to make tiles to decorate mosques, tombs and palaces in Central Asia.
at first it was used to make tiles to decorate mosques, tombs, and palaces in Central Asia.

claims.text: The statement of case says the art of blue pottery came to Jaipur from Persia and Afghanistan via the Mughal courts.

quotes.quote: The Art of blue pottery cnme to Jaipur from Persia and Afghanistan via Mughal Courts.

claims.text: The blue glaze technique grew beyond an architectural accessory to Kashmiri potters, reached the plains of Delhi and went to Jaipur in the 17th century.

quotes.quote: Gradually the blue glaze technique grew beyond an architectural accessory to Kashmiri potters.
From there, the technique traveled to the plains of Delhi
It travelled from Delhi to Jaipur in the 17th century.
it was later introduced in Delhi and moved to Jaipur artisans in the 17th century.

claims.text: The CBSE manual says blue pottery travelled from the Mughal courts to Rajasthan in 1562 as Akbar's gifts, including blue pottery made in Khurja, but the art developed only under Sawai Ram Singh I.

quotes.quote: The blue pottery travelled from Mughal courts to Rajasthan in 1562 when the Mughal ruler Akbar sent some gift items including vases of Mughal art or blue pottery made in khurja but the art could be developed only in the times of Sawai Ram Singh I

claims.text: The GI application says Man Singh I was the first to bring the art of blue and white to Jaipur, after his dealings with the Mughals and campaigns in Afghanistan.

quotes.quote: Man Singh I was the first to bring the art of blue and white to Jaipur subsequent to his interactions with the Mughals and through his campaigns in Afghanistan.

claims.text: The GI application says Man Singh I's introduction of blue and white to Jaipur was possibly temporary.

quotes.quote: through his campaigns in Afghanistan. This was possibly temporary.

claims.text: Maharaja Sawai Ram Singh II set up a school of art at Jaipur in 1866, and blue glaze pottery thrived primarily under its aegis.

quotes.quote: Sawai Ram Singh tr (1835-1880) set up a school of art in 1866
the School of Art was established in 1866 at Jaipur
Introduced in Jaipur from Delhi and Khurja by the ruler of Jaipur, Ram Singh II, blue glaze pottery thrived primarily under the aegis of the Jaipur School of Art, founded in 1866.

claims.text: Impart says Ram Singh II, ruler of Jaipur, introduced blue glaze pottery to Jaipur from Delhi and Khurja.

quotes.quote: Introduced in Jaipur from Delhi and Khurja by the ruler of Jaipur, Ram Singh II

claims.text: Under the reign of Sawai Ram Singh II, local artisans were sent to Delhi to be trained in the craft.

quotes.quote: under the reign of Sawai Ram Singh, local artisans were sent to Delhi to be trained in this Indian craft
Jaipur ruler Maharaja Sawai Ram Singh II was a great patron of the arts.
He sent artisans to Delhi to learn from the masters there.

claims.text: The Jaipur Museum Handbook stated that pottery of any value was not made in Jaipur until the School of Art opened in 1866.

quotes.quote: It was not until the opening of the School of Art in 1866 that pottery of any value was made in Jaipur

claims.text: The School of Art head potter's notes say a Delhi potter was the first to make pottery at the School, followed by a family of potters from Biana in Bharatpur State.

quotes.quote: A Delhi potter was the first to manufacture pottery at the School of Art. After him came a family of potters from Biana in the Bharatpur State, whose direct descendants still carry on the manufacture and the work of instruction at the institution.

claims.text: The V&A says the Jaipur School of Art produced pottery in the late 19th century after a pupil of Bhola, chief artist of Delhi fritware, introduced the technique.

quotes.quote: The school in Jaipur, Rajasthan, produced pottery in the late 19th century after one of the pupils of Bhola, who was a chief artist of Delhi fritware, introduced the technique.
The school, in Jaipur, produced pottery in the late 19th century after one of the pupils of Bhola, who was a chief artist of Delhi fritware, introduced the technique.

claims.text: Pickle jars called martabans, named after the Burmese fort through which they were imported, were copied first in Delhi and later at Jaipur.

quotes.quote: Pickle jars or martabans, as they were locally known, owing to the fort on the coast of Burma through which they were imported into India, were first copied in Delhi and later at Jaipur, where they were decorated in response to European taste.

claims.text: Under the School of Art's director Opendronath Sen, the pottery was displayed at the 1883 Jaipur Exhibition, encouraging a rise in local production.

quotes.quote: Under the institute's director, Opendronath Sen, the pottery was displayed at the 1883 Jaipur Exhibition, encouraging a rise in local production.

claims.text: Years of waning patronage and the advent of modern technologies forced blue glaze pottery into neglect and decline.

quotes.quote: However, years of waning patronage and the advent of modern technologies forced the art into neglect and decline.

claims.text: The statement of case says the craft was practised by one family who guarded its secrets, leading to lower standards and a gradual dying out.

quotes.quote: the craft was practiced by one family who guarded its secrets so closely and refused to share their trade secrets with their fellow craftsmen so there was an eventual lowering of standards and a gradual dying out of the craft

claims.text: It is largely believed that, because they were not popularised, the original blue pottery techniques were lost.

quotes.quote: Yet even during its revival, production techniques remained closely guarded secrets, and it is largely believed that because they were not popularized, the original blue pottery techniques were lost.

claims.text: The GI application says that when the Government of India suddenly closed the School of Art in 1957, Maharani Gayatri Devi of Jaipur gave the craft a third dose of life.

quotes.quote: In 1957, when the School that had started in 1866 was suddenly closed by the Government of India, it took a Maharani- Gayatri Devi of Jaipur- to inject a third dose of life

claims.text: The CBSE manual says blue pottery had almost vanished by the time of independence and the art school was closed down in 1954.

quotes.quote: The family gradually lost its hold and the art of blue pottery almost vanished by the time of independence. In 1954 the art school was closed down.

claims.text: A training school set up in 1963, named Sawai Ram Singh Shilp Kala Mandir, had Kripal Singh Shekhawat as its first director to train people in blue pottery.

quotes.quote: The school established in 1963 was named Sawai Ram Singh Shilp Kala Mandir and Shri Kripal Singh Shekhawat,a renowned artist of Rajasthan was made the first director of the school to train people in blue pottery.

claims.text: In the 1950s and after, Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay assigned Kripal Singh Shekhawat to research and develop the technique; Impart says the revival they led had support from Maharani Gayatri Devi.

quotes.quote: The social reformer and freedom fighter Ms.Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay assigned the task of researching and developing this pottery technique to a prominent artist, Mr. Kripal Singh Shekhawat.
During the post-Independence era of the 1950s and beyond, the pottery tradition was again revived, with success this time, by two women.
Successful attempts to revive the blue pottery industry were led by the social reformer Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay and artist Kirpal Singh Shekhawat, with support from Maharani Gayatri Devi.

claims.text: The statement of case says the craft received a much needed boost in the 1960's when the artist Kripal Singh Shekhawat entered the field.

quotes.quote: The craft received a much needed boost in the 1960's as intemationally renowned artist Kripal Singh Shekhawat entered the freld of Blue Pottery and raised the bar.

claims.text: Impart describes Kirpal Singh Shekhawat as principal of the Jaipur School of Art and says he referred to Albert Hall Museum artefacts and cenotaph tiles around Jaipur to re-establish the tradition.

quotes.quote: Kirpal Singh Shekhawat, principal of the Jaipur School of Art, referred to artefacts in the Albert Hall Museum, Jaipur, as well as the decorative tiles that clad cenotaphs around Jaipur, to re-establish the region's blue glaze pottery tradition.

claims.text: Kripal Singh Shekhawat of Rajasthan, a craftsman credited with reviving blue pottery, was conferred the Padma Shri in 1974 in the field of art.

quotes.quote: Shri Kirpal Singh Shekhawat RAJ PS24 Art
Kripal Singh Shekhawat, a renowned craftsman who revived Blue Pottery and was conferred with the Padma Shri in 1974.

claims.text: Khushboo Bharti writes that the Maharani Gayatri Devi girls' school was the first educational institute to support teaching Jaipur pottery techniques, with a proper studio and kiln.

quotes.quote: MGD girls' school was the first educational institute to support the teaching of the Jaipur pottery techniques by creating a proper pottery studio with a kiln.

claims.text: Jaipur's rulers were partial to blue-glazed ware, and marble halls in Rambagh Palace have fountains lined with blue tiles as centrepieces.

quotes.quote: The rulers of Jaipur were exceptionally partial to blue-glazed ware, and many marble halls in Rambagh Palace has as its centre piece a bubbling fountain lined with ravishing blue tiles.
There are, however, numerous evidences still extant in the architecture of Jaipur to show that the early rulers of Jaipur had a great liking for porcelain tiles.

claims.text: The GI application says the Mughals first wanted the tiles for mosques resembling Persia's, while the Jaipur Maharajas revived the craft for architectural extravagance.

quotes.quote: When the technique arrived in the country, the purpose was religious as the Mughals wanted tiles to be made for the mosques, resembling those of Persia.
But it's revival in Jaipur, by the Maharajas, was with a purpose of achieving architectural extravagance

claims.text: The GI application says that as royal patronage declined, artisans turned to more mundane and utility products to capture middle-class customers.

quotes.quote: Slowly with the decline in the royal patronage, the artisans resorted to more mundane and utility products, trying to capture the middle class

claims.text: Impart says Jaipur blue glaze pottery emerged in the nineteenth century, with designs developed from Delhi and Khurja workshops of the Sultanate period.

quotes.quote: Emerging in the nineteenth century, the designs found on blue glaze pottery in Jaipur were developed based on ceramics from the workshops of Delhi and Khurja (in present-day Uttar Pradesh) that were established during the Sultanate period.

claims.text: The Mughals' chini-khanas, which housed their collections of Chinese and Persian pottery, provided inspiration for the artisans.

quotes.quote: The impressive collections of the wealthy Mughals served as a reference point for the revival of the art.
Their assorted chini-khanas that housed their collections of Chinese and Persian pottery provided inspiration for the artisans.

claims.text: The Journal of Indian Art judged Jaipur ware practically the same as Delhi pottery but in some respects an improvement upon it.

quotes.quote: It has already been stated that the Jaipur ware is practically the same as that of Delhi; but it is, in some respects, an improvement upon it.

claims.text: The Journal of Indian Art describes Jaipur ware as fine white pottery with a thick semi-translucent glaze, the same as Ancient Egypt's Ushabti figures.

quotes.quote: It is fine white pottery with a thick semi-translucent glaze, and (as was pointed out some years ago, we think by Sir George Birdwood) it is really the same as that of the well-known Ushabti figures of Ancient Egypt.

claims.text: The head potter's notes describe the designs on Jaipur pottery as usually conventional and mythological.

quotes.quote: The designs - are usually conventional and mythological.

claims.text: The design is first sketched in pencil on the surface, then outlined with cobalt oxide and filled in with other oxides by colour.

quotes.quote: A sketch of the design is first done in pencil on the clay's surface, then outlined with cobalt oxide, and finally filled in with other oxides according to color.
The design is then applied onto the treated surface of the piece, rendered first in pencil and then with paint.

claims.text: The GI application says traditional motifs such as tessellating jaali, all-over motifs and stylised floral designs reflect the pottery's Persian origins.

quotes.quote: The traditional motifs like tessellating type ot iaali, all over motifs and the stylized floral designs reflect their Persian origins.
The traditional motifs like tessellating type ofjaali, all over the motifs and the stylized floral designs reflect socio-cultural history

claims.text: The GI application says most items are domestic kitchenware such as cups, plates, flower vases and tea pots, with small items such as door knobs and tiles, and artisans have started making buttons and costume jewellery.

quotes.quote: Most of the items comprise of domestic kitchenware such as cups, plates, flower vases, tea pots, urns, tea coasters, napkin holders, bread holder.
Also small items such as table top accessories, door knobs, pen stands, paper weights, tiles, incense stick stands, candle stands, bathroom fittings
The artisans have started making even buttons and costume jewellery

claims.text: Flower patterns and geometric designs, both common in the Islamic arts from which Jaipur pottery evolved, are common motifs, but animals such as elephants and peacocks also recur.

quotes.quote: Many of the common motifs in Jaipur pottery are flower patterns or geometric designs-both are commonly seen in the Islamic arts from which Jaipur pottery evolved, but animals such as elephants and peacocks are also recurring images.

claims.text: The statement of case lists nine major steps: dough preparation, glaze making, fabrication, adding the base, finishing, white engobe, painting, kiln loading and firing.

quotes.quote: The production of the blue pottery of Jaipur in Rajasthan involves basically major nine steps. These are Preparation of dough, Glaze making, Bharan nikaalna (Fabrication of the wares), Pendi lagana (addition of the base)
Rezmaal ka kaam (finishing), Engobe/Astaar lagana (application of white base color), Rangaai (painting design), Bharana/bhatti ko jamana (loading of articles in the kiln), Pakana (Firing).

claims.text: The GI application form says production involves basically eleven steps, but the list it gives names nine, from preparation of dough to firing.

quotes.quote: basically eleven steps to name: Preparation of dough Glaze Making Bharan nikaalna (Fabrication of the wares) Pendi lagana (addition of the base)
Rezmaal ka kaam (finishing) Engobe/Asfaar lagana (application of white base color) Rangaai (painting design Bharana/bhatti ko jamana (loading of articles in the kiln) Pakana (Firing)

claims.text: The CBSE manual divides the process into twelve main steps, from making the dough and moulds through casting, finishing, painting and glazing to firing.

quotes.quote: The whole process can be divided into following main steps; 1. Making of the Dough 2. Making of the Molds 3. Casting of the Products 4. Scrubbing 5. Finishing 6. Attaching the Base 7. Smoothening 8. Designing 9. Colour Making 10. Painting 11. Glazing 12. Firing

claims.text: The dough is made from ground quartz, glass (kaanch), katira gond, multani mitti (fuller's earth) and saaji (soda bicarbonate).

quotes.quote: The base mixture consists of ground quartz stone, Kaanch (glass), Katira Gond (edible gum), Multani Mitti (Fuller's Earth), Saaji (soda bicarbonate), and Maida (flour), which is used for coating and occasionally as a substitute for Fuller's Earth.
Saaji (soda bicarbonate), Multan mitti (Fuller's earth), Kaatira gond (natural resin)

claims.text: The head potter's notes list locally obtained quartz stone, kach (glass), sajjt (borax), katira (gum) and Multani matt, Multan clay or fuller's earth, as the materials of Jaipur pottery.

quotes.quote: Stone (quartz locally obtained)
Kach (glass) es ia sk oa TE ... I} seer Sajjt (borax) fis ae er Katira (gum)
Multani matt (Multan clay, or fuller's earth)

claims.text: At one Jaipur family workshop the dough is roughly 1 part each of gum, rock salt and fuller's earth to 7 parts glass and 40 parts quartz.

quotes.quote: The other ingredients are quartz, glass, rock salt, and gum.
The ratios are roughly 1 part each of gum, salt, and clay (Fullers Earth, which is usually bentonite, kaolinite, montmorillonite, and attapulgite): 7 parts glass: 40 parts quartz.

claims.text: One Jaipur potter calls the prepared body dough rather than a clay body, because clay ingredients make up only one part of the recipe.

quotes.quote: Doraya refers to preparing the materials as making dough, rather than making a clay body, because the ingredients in a typical clay body constitute only one part of the recipe.

claims.text: At one workshop the raw materials are mixed with water and left overnight, then kneaded to a uniform consistency and rested 2-3 days before use.

quotes.quote: The raw materials are mixed with water and left overnight. The next day they are kneaded together into a uniform consistency and again left for 2-3 days before use.

claims.text: The School of Art head potter's notes describe pulverising and sieving the materials through wire gauze, then working them with water into a soft paste like bread dough.

quotes.quote: pulverized, and reduced to a fine-grained powder by means of a wire gauze sieve.
Sufficient water is poured over it to produce a soft paste-like composition
This composition is very similar to the kneaded flour prepared for making bread.

claims.text: The dough is rolled and flattened into a chapati about 4-5 millimetre thick and placed in a mould.

quotes.quote: It is then rolled and flattened into a 4-5 millimetre thick 'Chapatti' (pancake) and placed in moulds
a round shape like chapatti with an approximate thickness of 4-5 mm.

claims.text: D'Source describes the dough flattened with a flattening tool into a round roti-like shape about 1cm thick.

quotes.quote: A good amount of dough is flattened to a round roti like shape of approximate 1cm thickness with a flattening tool.

claims.text: The dough-lined mould is packed with dry ash, or raakh, so that the dough takes the exact shape of the mould.

quotes.quote: The hollow empty spaces of the moulds are then packed with dry ashes.
They fill the inside of the mold with raakh or burnt wood ash to fit the chappati to the mold from the inside out
The mold with dough in it is then filled with burnt wood dust and pressed gently so that dough takes the exact shape of the mold.

claims.text: The moulded piece dries for 1-2 days with the ash inside, after which the ash is brushed off with a small broom.

quotes.quote: The product is left for drying for 1-2 days along with burnt wood dust in itself.
After it has dried completely, the excess raakh is brushed off using akoochi or small broom.

claims.text: Moulds are made from plaster of Paris in the desired shapes and, if maintained properly, can be used many times.

quotes.quote: Molds are made from Plaster of Paris (POP).
The molds if maintained properly can be used for more numbers of times.

claims.text: The School of Art head potter's notes describe moulds made of clay and baked before use, with the moulded contents emptied onto a slab and dried in the sun.

quotes.quote: The moulds are made of clay and are baked before use. The soft contents of the mould are emptied on to a slab and dried in the sun.

claims.text: At one workshop the foot is thrown directly onto the dried, upturned form on a potter's wheel instead of being made in a plaster mould.

quotes.quote: Rather than making a foot with a plaster mold, the dried, plaster-cast form is placed upside down on a potter's wheel and the foot is thrown directly onto the form.

claims.text: Products such as vases are given a base for stability, attached with some dough and sprinkled with water until leather hard.

quotes.quote: Products like vases are provided with base to give them stability. The base is attached to the product with some amount of dough and sprinkled with water to make it leather hard.

claims.text: A vase is made in four parts, a wheel-turned neck, two moulded hemispheres and a wheel-turned base, which are joined and smoothed over.

quotes.quote: A vase, for example, will be made up in four parts; a wheel-turned neck; two moulded hemispheres; and a wheel-turned base.
All these four parts are joined together using the dough and the surface is smoothed.

claims.text: The rough edges of the dried piece are rubbed smooth on stone, and the piece is then rubbed with sandpaper to make its surface even.

quotes.quote: The rough edge of the product is smoothened by rubbing it on stone gently. After this, the product is rubbed with the sandpaper to remove grains and to make surface of product even.

claims.text: Any holes the ash may have left are filled with a slurry of dough and water, and the piece is dried and sanded again.

quotes.quote: the dried pieces are smoothed with a slurry mixture of dough and water to fill any holes on the surface that may have been caused by the ash placed in the mold during drying.
The product is coated with, dough mixed with water to fill the pores and later the product is dried and rubbed with sandpaper again.

claims.text: Before painting, the piece is coated with a mixture of quartz powder, powdered glass, maida flour and water, then dried.

quotes.quote: the pieces are again coated by hand with a slip that is a mixture of quartz powder, powdered glass, and edible flour called maida.
It is then dried after being immersed in a solution of quartz powder, powdered glass, edible refined flour (maida), and water.

claims.text: The statement of case says outlines are drawn in cobalt oxide with a squirrel-tail brush that painters make themselves from the tails of ground squirrels.

quotes.quote: The outlines are drawn in cobalt oxide using a squirel-tail brush (little ground squirrels are frequently run over, and the painten collect the tails, from which they make their own brushed).

claims.text: On circular pieces a neat outline is drawn by placing the piece on a potter's wheel and touching the brush tip to it.

quotes.quote: If the product is circular shape then the outline is easy to give, product is just placed on potter's wheel and by touching the tip of brush to the product a neat line could be drawn.

claims.text: The colouring oxides are mixed with edible gum, which acts as a binding agent, and crushed on stone before being brushed on.

quotes.quote: In order to create the underglaze colors, oxides are mixed with gum, which acts as a binding agent.
These oxides are combined with edible gum and crushed on the stone before being applied with a brush.

claims.text: The glaze coat must be even, since too thick a coat gives a matte finish and too thin a coat leaves the pores exposed.

quotes.quote: the coat of product should not be too thick or thin, and it should be evenly coated. Too thick will give matte finish and when it is too thin it will leave the pores exposed.

claims.text: Pieces are stacked in the kiln so they do not touch, the kiln is closed from the top, and the open centre lets heat from wood and charcoal circulate.

quotes.quote: The products are properly stacked inside so that it doesn't touch each other.

The kiln is closed from top and heating is done from below using wood and charcoal, and an even circulation of heat within the kiln is maintained by leaving the center core open for heat to move freely.

claims.text: The CBSE manual warns that products stuck to each other in the kiln risk turning black, so stacking is done with utmost care.

quotes.quote: The stacking is done with utmost care so that no two products stick to each other
If products stick to each other there are possibilities of them turning black.

claims.text: Pieces are fired at 800-850° C for six hours in a closed kiln fuelled with charcoal.

quotes.quote: they are frred at 800 - 8500 C for six hours in a closed kiln fuelled with charcoal.
the object is baked in a kiln at 800-850° C for six hours.

claims.text: Ceramics Monthly reports that one Jaipur workshop fires its wood-fired kiln in oxidation for 8 hours to 1000°C.

quotes.quote: It is a wood-fired kiln with a small pit located right in front of the small opening where they throw the wood inside, with smaller stoke holes around the base.
It is fired in oxidation for 8 hours to 1832°F (1000°C).

claims.text: Firing takes 4-5 hours and is kept gradual, because changes in temperature might cause cracks in the products.

quotes.quote: The firing takes place for 4-5 hours and the firing has to be controlled to be gradual because changes in temperature might cause cracks in products.

claims.text: One artisan family bakes its pieces at 750 to 850 degrees Celsius for about five hours and opens the furnace only on the third day.

quotes.quote: It is then placed in the furnace and baked at 750 to 850 degrees Celsius.
They are then fired for about five hours and left to cool the next day. The furnace is opened only on the third day,

claims.text: The kiln is left to cool for about three days, avoiding rapid temperature changes that easily crack the ware.

quotes.quote: The kiln is left to cool for three days, avoiding any rapid temperature change which so easily cracks the china.
They are allowed to cool in the kiln for about three days, and are then removed, being ready for use.
is then cooled for about three days before it is considered a finished product.

claims.text: The Federal reports that firing relies on locally sourced, seasoned khezadi wood, with charcoal among the other essential materials.

quotes.quote: The firing process relies on locally sourced, seasoned Khezadi wood, while other essential ingredients include charcoal, water, borax powder, zinc oxide, potassium nitrate, and boric acid-each contributing to its unique texture.

claims.text: In certain regions diesel furnaces have replaced traditional wood or charcoal-fuelled kilns, and the new furnaces in use are diesel and gas powered.

quotes.quote: In certain regions, diesel furnaces have replaced traditional wood or charcoal-fueled kilns.
The new furnaces being used are diesel and gas powered.

claims.text: The traditional kiln resembles a dome whose door, also its chimney, sits at the apex in the middle of the dome.

quotes.quote: most closely resembling a geodesic dome, the door of the kiln is also its chimney and is located right at the apex in the middle of the dome.

claims.text: One artisan family says its manufacturing ratio is 50:50, so only half of the items remain fit for sale after firing.

quotes.quote: The manufacturing ratio is 50:50, meaning that only half of the items remain fit for sale after being baked in the furnace.

claims.text: The Federal reports that the craft has a high damage ratio of 30-40%, and any breakage after firing means starting again.

quotes.quote: the craft comes with challenges, including a high damage ratio of 30-40%.
any post-firing breakage means starting from scratch.

claims.text: Once made, blue pottery items cannot be reworked, and the smallest mistake could lead a piece to crack up or turn black.

quotes.quote: Once made, the blue pottery items cannot b€ reworked.
The smallest mistake could lead to the piece either cracking up or tuming black.

claims.text: A Kot Jewar artisan family told The Federal that a piece of blue pottery takes around 15 days to complete, whether a single plate or a batch of one hundred.

quotes.quote: Creating a single piece of blue pottery takes around 15 days to complete, whether it's a single plate or a batch of one hundred.

claims.text: One Kot Jewar workshop names its tools regmaal (sandpaper), patti (iron blade), koochi (broom), chaak (potter's wheel) and bhatti (kiln).

quotes.quote: Other key instruments include Regmaal (sandpaper in 60, 100, and 180 grades), the Patti (iron blade/knife), Saancha (iron cutter), Koochi (broom), Chaak (potter's wheel), brushes, and the Bhatti (heating kiln).

claims.text: Blue Pottery of Jaipur was filed for registration as geographical indication application 66 by the Development Commissioner (Handicrafts) on 14 August 2006.

claims.text: The registry issued certificate number 74 on 10 July 2008, after the application appeared in Geographical Indications Journal Supp 1, available from 24 March 2008.

quotes.quote: | Journal Number | Supp 1 | | Availability Date | 24-03-2008 | | Certificate Number | 74 | | Certificate Date | 10-07-2008 |

claims.text: The registry record lists Blue Pottery of Jaipur with the status Registered and gives the registration as valid up to 13 August 2026.

quotes.quote: | Geographical Indications | Blue Pottery of Jaipur | | Status | Registered |
| Registration Valid Upto | 13-08-2026 |

claims.text: The GI registry's record of application 66 lists 160 authorised users of the Blue Pottery of Jaipur geographical indication.

quotes.quote: | Sl.No. | Authorized User No | Authorized User Name | Authorized User Address | Status |

claims.text: Urvashi Dev Rawal's feature reports that blue pottery is historically linked to Jaipur and got the geographical indication tag in 2006.

quotes.quote: it is historically linked to Jaipur and even got the Geographical Indication or GI tag in 2006.

claims.text: NABARD says Jaipur's blue pottery was registered under GI in 2006 with its support, and that it registered artisans as authorised users.

quotes.quote: it was registered under GI in 2006 with support from NABARD. The organisation also took the initiative to register artisans/producers of this community as authorized users.

claims.text: Impart says Jaipur's blue glaze pottery received a GI tag in 2008, while workshops making similar wares have cropped up elsewhere, such as Chinhat near Lucknow.

quotes.quote: Jaipur's blue glaze pottery received a Geographical Indication (GI) tag in 2008, and while the industry remains protected in Jaipur, several other workshops producing similar wares have cropped up in regions such as Chinhat near Lucknow in present-day Uttar Pradesh.

claims.text: A logo for Blue Pottery of Jaipur was filed separately as GI application 540 by the Development Commissioner (Handicraft) on 28 December 2015.

quotes.quote: | Application Number | 540 | | Geographical Indications | Blue Pottery of Jaipur (Logo) | | Status | Registered | | Applicant Name | Development Commissioner (Handicraft) |

claims.text: The logo was registered with certificate number 293 on 29 April 2017, after publication in Geographical Indications Journal 93, and its record gives validity up to 27 December 2025.

quotes.quote: | Journal Number | 93 | | Availability Date | 30-11-2016 | | Certificate Number | 293 | | Certificate Date | 29-04-2017 |
| Registration Valid Upto | 27-12-2025 |

claims.text: The logo's statement of case says producers in other areas and other countries sell similar goods as Blue Pottery of Jaipur to earn its premium price.

quotes.quote: The producers of other area and even producers of other countries are making the similar typ€ print and selling in the name of Blue pottery of Jaipur for deriving premium price associated with it

claims.text: The GI application says artisans are forced to keep low rates because the pottery competes with cheap factory-made look-alikes.

quotes.quote: And since they stand competition from the factory made cheap look-alikes, the artisans are forced to keep low rates.

claims.text: The Jaipur School of Art catalogue for 1905 priced its pottery from four annas for a small menu-holder to five and a half rupees for a twenty-inch vase.

quotes.quote: The Jaipur School of Art Catalogue for 1905 contains five plates of illustrations of no fewer than eighty-seven separate specimens of pottery varying in price from a small menu-holder at four annas to a vase twenty inches high at five and a half rupees.

claims.text: A legend in the GI application tells that a potter named Churamani beat the Maharaja's kite master with a kite string coated in glass dust from his pottery.

quotes.quote: There is a story/legend which tells of how Maharaja
Maharaja's kite master was defeated by a potter called Churamani, who had coated his kite string with glass dust of his blue green pottery.

claims.text: One Jaipur pottery family's story says two forefathers cut the Maharaja's kite and, being potters from Iran or Iraq, made pottery to appease him.

quotes.quote: One day, two of his family members came to Jaipur and were flying a kite. They ended up crossing and cutting the Maharaja's kite. The Maharaja discovered that they were potters from Iran/Iraq and they ended up making pottery for the Maharaja to appease him after ruining his kite.

claims.text: Blue pottery was once believed to have let Mughal kings detect poisoned food, a change in the glaze colour showing the food was tampered with.

quotes.quote: The craft, which flourished under Mughal patronage, was once believed to serve a more utilitarian purpose-detecting poisoned food.
Mughal kings used blue pottery to check their food. If the colour of the glaze changed, it conveyed that the food had been tampered with, or poisoned.

claims.text: The statement of case and the CBSE manual trace Jaipur's blue pottery to two brothers from Achnera near Agra, whom the CBSE manual names Churaman and Kaluram, adding that Churaman headed the School's blue pottery section in 1866.

quotes.quote: watched as his kite masters were engaged in battle with two brothers from Achnera (near Agra.) who were to father the turquoise blue pottery of Jaipur.
When the ruler saw the two brothers Churaman and Kaluram managed to bring down the royal kites almost every time
Thus their family migrated from Achnera and settled down in the Ganga Meharon ki Gali within the four walls of the pink city.
In 1866 Maharaja Sawai Ram Singh II established his school of arts and industries in Kishanpol Bazar and Churaman was made the head of the bluepottery section.

claims.text: A Kot Jewar potter told Urvashi Dev Rawal that Kot Jewar was once a hub of blue pottery, and that at other centres like Jaipur, Mahla and Nevta the units shut down with time.

quotes.quote: Prajapati says Kot Jewar was once a hub of Blue Pottery. There were other centres like Jaipur, Mahla, and Nevta but with time the units shut down.

claims.text: One artisan family told Urvashi Dev Rawal that its glaze is a mixture of sindoor, borax and glass powder, melted at 1200 degrees Celsius, cooled in water and ground fine.

quotes.quote: The final step is to glaze the artefact using a mixture of sindoor, borax and glass powder. This mixture is melted in the furnace at 1200 degrees Celsius, then cooled in water and ground into a fine powder.

lede.text: Blue pottery of Jaipur is completely hand painted, its GI documents describe it as based on ground quartz, and its blue from cobalt oxide is so dominant that it is easily recognised.

The statement of case names families in Jaipur and in villages such as Neota, Muhana, Mahalan and Kot Jewar, while a Kot Jewar potter says that at other centres like Jaipur, Mahla and Nevta the units shut down with time.
Turko-Persian in origin, the blue glaze technique travelled to India in the 14th century, and in Jaipur blue glaze pottery thrived under the School of Art founded in 1866.

keyFacts.label: GI status
keyFacts.value: Registered, application 66 filed 14 August 2006, certificate 74 dated 10 July 2008; NABARD and one feature give 2006 as the registration year

keyFacts.label: Centres
keyFacts.value: Jaipur, and Neota, Muhana, Mahalan and Kot Jewar in Jaipur district by the GI documents; a Kot Jewar potter says units at Jaipur, Mahla and Nevta shut down

keyFacts.label: Body
keyFacts.value: Ground quartz with glass, fuller's earth, katira gond and saaji; sources differ on clay, feldspar and what saaji is

keyFacts.label: Colours
keyFacts.value: Cobalt-oxide blue and copper turquoise; sources differ on whether green comes from chromium or copper

keyFacts.label: Firing
keyFacts.value: Fired once; 800-850° C for six hours by the statement of case and Impart, 1000°C at one workshop

keyFacts.label: Steps
keyFacts.value: Nine in the GI documents (the form says eleven but lists nine); twelve in the CBSE manual

keyFacts.label: Revival
keyFacts.value: Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay and Kripal Singh Shekhawat (Padma Shri 1974), with support from Maharani Gayatri Devi

keyFacts.label: GI logo
keyFacts.value: Application 540, certificate 293 dated 29 April 2017; its record gives validity up to 27 December 2025

sentences.text: Blue glaze on pottery was first developed by Mongol artisans who combined Chinese glazing technology with Persian decorative arts, and in its infancy it made tiles to decorate mosques, tombs and palaces in Central Asia.

Sources differ on when it came to Jaipur: Ceramics Monthly and Outlook Traveller have the technique reaching Jaipur in the 17th century, while the Jaipur Museum Handbook stated that pottery of any value was not made there until the School of Art opened in 1866.

Sources differ on the School's first potters: the head potter's notes name a Delhi potter followed by a family from Biana, the V&A a pupil of Bhola of Delhi, and the statement of case and the CBSE manual two brothers from Achnera near Agra, Churaman and Kaluram.
Under the director Opendronath Sen the pottery was displayed at the 1883 Jaipur Exhibition, encouraging a rise in local production.
Years of waning patronage and the advent of modern technologies forced the art into decline, and the statement of case says the craft was practised by one family who guarded its secrets.
The school closed in 1957 according to the GI application and in 1954 according to the CBSE manual.

Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay assigned the artist Kripal Singh Shekhawat to research and develop the technique, in a revival Impart says had support from Maharani Gayatri Devi, and he was conferred the Padma Shri in 1974.

The statement of case lists nine major steps, from preparing the dough and making the glaze through fabrication, the base, finishing, white engobe and painting to loading the kiln and firing, while the GI application form says eleven but lists the same nine, and the CBSE manual counts twelve.
The dough is flattened into a chapati, 4-5 millimetre thick by some accounts and about 1cm by D'Source, and placed in plaster of Paris moulds packed with burnt wood ash.
After 1-2 days of drying the ash is brushed off, and products such as vases are given a base attached with some dough and water.
The piece is smoothed on stone and with sandpaper, holes are filled with a slurry of dough and water, and it is coated with quartz powder, powdered glass, maida and water before painting.
The design is sketched in pencil, outlined in cobalt oxide with a squirrel-tail brush and filled in with other metal oxides.
After painting, the piece is dipped in glaze and set in the sun to dry.

Blue pottery needs only one firing for baking and glazing, and sources differ on that firing, given as 800-850° C for six hours by the statement of case and Impart and as 8 hours to 1000°C at one workshop.
The kiln then cools for about three days, or for 2-3 days by other accounts.
On firing, the oxide of cobalt becomes a deep blue, cadmium produces a bright yellow and iron oxide becomes a red-brown.

Sources differ on green: the statement of case, Impart, Ceramics Monthly and The Federal give chromium, while the Journal of Indian Art, a V&A record of a jar of about 1880 and the CBSE manual give copper oxide, which the Journal says was found with the cobalt in the same mines.
A solid turquoise ground is made with copper oxide and gum, and the colouring oxides are mixed with edible gum as a binding agent.
In the glaze, borax reduces the melting point of the raw materials heated at a high temperature.
The statement of case says 80 per cent of the quartz is left after firing and maintains the form of the vessel.

The dough is made from ground quartz, glass, katira gond, multani mitti (fuller's earth) and saaji, which the statement of case and The Federal give as soda bicarbonate, while the head potter's notes list sajjt (borax).
At one family workshop the dough is roughly 1 part each of gum, rock salt and fuller's earth to 7 parts glass and 40 parts quartz.
Older records differ: the Jaipur Museum Handbook gave clay and felspar as the principal ingredients, and the V&A describes School of Art pieces made of feldspar and starch.
Sources differ on the sindoor in the glaze: the statement of case gives it as red lead, while the head potter's notes and Impart give vermilion.
Blue came from cobalt oxides originally mined in the principality of Khetri, purple from a stone called saind found in Bharatpur district, and yellow from lead, pewter and sandstone from Karauli.

Sources differ on whether the glaze still contains lead: a 2003 CGCRI paper reports that its intervention eliminated lead from blue pottery, while the statement of case of the 2015 logo application lists lead oxide and sindoor (red lead) in the glaze.
The Federal reports that modern techniques have shifted towards lead-free coatings, while one artisan family describes its glaze as a mixture of sindoor, borax and glass powder.
The CGCRI paper reports that blue pottery suffered from lead in its body and glaze compositions and from water leakage due to high porosity, fragility and glaze blackening.
The GI application calls the pottery suitable and hygienic for daily use, while the Rough Guide to India warns that it should not be used for hot food.
In a survey of 30 male workers, every worker reported discomfort in the lower back and knee, and poor postures carry a high risk of musculoskeletal disorders.

The Development Commissioner (Handicrafts) filed application 66 on 14 August 2006 and the registry issued certificate number 74 on 10 July 2008, while NABARD and a feature by Urvashi Dev Rawal give 2006 as the year of registration.
The registry lists 160 authorised users and records the status as Registered, with the registration valid up to 13 August 2026.
A logo was filed separately as application 540 and registered with certificate number 293 on 29 April 2017.
The GI application says artisans are forced to keep low rates because of competition from cheap factory-made look-alikes.
The Jaipur School of Art catalogue for 1905 priced its pottery from four annas for a small menu-holder to five and a half rupees for a twenty-inch vase.
Traditional motifs include tessellating jaali, all-over motifs and stylised floral designs, which the GI application says reflect Persian origins.
Flower patterns and geometric designs are common motifs, but animals such as elephants and peacocks also recur.
The GI application says most items are domestic kitchenware such as cups, plates, flower vases and tea pots, and that artisans have started making buttons and costume jewellery.
The Mughals' chini-khanas of Chinese and Persian pottery provided inspiration for the artisans.
The GI application says the quartz composition of the ceramic is well suited to the hot and dry climate of the area.

The Federal reports that production halts during the monsoon because the traditional technique relies on sun-drying, and the CBSE manual lists dependency on the sun for drying among the industry's problems.
In Kot Jewar, pieces dry in the abundant sunlight on the rooftops and courtyards of artists' homes.
